description: How the Wall Street Crash reshaped European politics and unravelled 1920s internationalism.
content_html:
The Wall Street Crash and Its Global Reach

On 24 October 1929 — a day known as Black Thursday — the New York stock market began a catastrophic collapse. Share prices continued to fall through to late November, wiping out fortunes and triggering bank failures across the United States. Within months, the effects had spread far beyond American borders, producing an economic crisis of a scale and depth the world had not previously experienced.

Key Fact

The international connection was critical. The Dawes Plan of 1924 had created a circular system: US banks lent money to Germany, Germany paid reparations to France and Britain, France and Britain repaid their war debts to the USA. When American banks recalled their loans after October 1929, this cycle broke down instantly. German unemployment rose from approximately 1.3 million in 1929 to roughly 6 million by 1932.

The Retreat to Economic Nationalism

Governments responded to the Depression by trying to protect their domestic economies, but this drove nations further apart. In June 1930, the US Congress passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, raising import taxes to record levels. Other countries retaliated with their own tariff increases, and international trade contracted sharply throughout the early 1930s. The League of Nations’ World Economic Conference of 1933 failed to produce any coordinated response.

Britain abandoned the gold standard in September 1931, devaluing the pound to make exports cheaper. Other countries followed, leading to a series of competitive devaluations that destabilised currencies globally. These economic decisions made international co-operation harder, as each government prioritised domestic recovery over international obligations.

Political Consequences in Europe

The Depression created the conditions in which extremist political movements could grow. In Germany, the economic catastrophe transformed the political landscape. The Nazi Party, which had received only 2.6 per cent of the vote in the 1928 Reichstag elections, rose to 37.4 per cent in July 1932 as unemployed workers and anxious middle-class voters turned to radical alternatives. On 30 January 1933, President Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler as Chancellor of Germany.

In Italy, Mussolini’s Fascist government exploited the Depression to advance autarky — national economic self-sufficiency through state control of production and reduced dependence on foreign trade. In Hungary, Austria, and Romania, authoritarian governments replaced parliamentary democracies. These shifts made collective action through the League of Nations increasingly difficult.

The Depression’s political consequences were not confined to Europe. Japan’s economy was severely damaged by falling demand for its exports. On 18 September 1931, officers of the Japanese Kwantung Army staged the Mukden incident — fabricating a pretext to invade Manchuria. The Japanese government’s civilian leaders were unable to restrain the military, and by 1932 Japan had established the puppet state of Manchukuo across the whole of Manchuria. China appealed to the League of Nations. The League’s Lytton Commission of Inquiry condemned the invasion but recommended only that Japan evacuate Manchuria and accept League supervision. Japan refused, and in March 1933 withdrew from the League entirely. This was the first major test of the collective security system, and it failed.

The German Political Crisis

Germany’s political system came under unbearable strain between 1930 and 1933. Chancellor Heinrich Brüning adopted deflationary policies — cutting government spending and wages — which worsened unemployment in the short term and were politically catastrophic. Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed the President to govern by emergency decree, and it was used with increasing frequency as the Reichstag became ungovernable.

Between January 1932 and January 1933, Germany had three different chancellors. Extreme parties at both ends of the political spectrum — the Nazi Party on the far right and the Communist Party of Germany on the far left — gained seats while centre parties collapsed. Conservative politicians around President von Hindenburg believed they could use Hitler as a tool and later control him. This miscalculation led directly to his appointment as Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

Key Fact

By 1933 the Depression had produced three interconnected threats to the international order: Germany had a fascist government with no commitment to Versailles; Japan had openly defied the League and left it; and the economic nationalism triggered by Smoot-Hawley had dissolved the trade relationships that had underpinned European stability in the 1920s.

Historians debate how far the Depression automatically produced authoritarian outcomes. Some argue the economic crisis created the conditions but not the certainty: democratic governments in France, Britain, and Scandinavia survived the Depression without collapsing into authoritarianism, suggesting that political institutions, civic traditions, and leadership choices also mattered. Others point to structural factors — Germany’s short democratic experience since 1919, its hyperinflation trauma of 1923, the humiliating legacy of Versailles — that made it more vulnerable than its western neighbours. This debate matters for the exam: framing the Nazi rise as the inevitable product of capitalism failing is too simple and does not reflect the range of historical opinion.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the Depression and the retreat to nationalism, avoid treating the Wall Street Crash and Hitler’s rise as a simple cause-and-effect chain. Examiners look for multi-causal analysis: the Dawes Plan dependency, the Smoot-Hawley tariff, the failure of the 1933 World Economic Conference, the Manchurian crisis, and the specific political weaknesses of Weimar Germany all played roles. The time-frame discipline noted in the examiner reports applies here: if a question specifies the Depression’s impact, stay within the 1929–1933 period and do not run on into 1930s crises.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 broke the Dawes Plan circular flow, causing German unemployment to reach roughly 6 million by 1932 and creating the conditions for political extremism.
  • Governments responded with economic nationalism — Smoot-Hawley tariffs, competitive devaluations, abandonment of the gold standard — which dissolved the international cooperation of the 1920s.
  • By 1933, Germany had a Nazi government, Japan had defied and left the League over Manchuria, and collective security had been shown to be ineffective against determined aggressors.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the Wall Street Crash of 1929 affected Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each effect scores 1 mark for identification and 1 for specific detail. Examples: US banks recalled loans to Germany (1), causing the Dawes Plan circular payment system to collapse (1); German unemployment rose from approximately 1.3 million (1929) to roughly 6 million by 1932 (1); the Nazi Party's vote share rose from 2.6% (1928) to 37.4% (July 1932) (1) as desperate voters sought radical alternatives (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 damaged international relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed with causal analysis — it triggered retaliatory tariff increases from other countries (trade wars contracting global commerce); it damaged economic interdependence that had underpinned 1920s stability, making international co-operation harder when crises arose. Secure: Both explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained, one identified. Emerging: General statement about economic nationalism without specific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the political crisis in Germany between 1930 and 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature plus 1 for detail. Feature 1: The Nazi Party's electoral support surged (1); from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932 as economic hardship grew (1). Feature 2: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution was used increasingly to govern by emergency decree (1); bypassing the Reichstag and weakening parliamentary democracy (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Great Depression made it harder for the League of Nations to maintain international order.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Multiple interlocking causes — economic nationalism (Smoot-Hawley) reduced co-operation; the Manchurian crisis showed the League could not act decisively; the rise of authoritarian governments hostile to collective security weakened the League's membership; Britain and France were too focused on domestic recovery to take strong action abroad. Connects causes to show systemic undermining of collective security. Secure: Two or more causes with explanation. Developing: One cause explained, others listed. Emerging: General reference to the Depression without causal link to the League.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of why authoritarian governments rose in Europe after 1929. Interpretation A argues the Depression was the decisive cause, removing economic stability and driving desperate populations towards extremist movements. Interpretation B contends that pre-existing political weaknesses — such as Versailles grievances and short democratic traditions — were equally important. How far do the interpretations differ and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies that Interpretation A emphasises economic causation while B focuses on structural/historical factors; uses own knowledge (Weimar's hyperinflation legacy, Versailles resentment, Smoot-Hawley consequences) to support both; explains why historians disagree (which factors they weight most). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Notes some differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was the Wall Street Crash the main cause of the breakdown of international order between 1929 and 1933? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Wall Street Crash (Dawes Plan collapse, German unemployment, extremist politics) against other factors (pre-existing Versailles grievances, Smoot-Hawley tariff choices, Japanese militarism, League structural weakness); draws on named interpretations or schools where possible; reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: Clear argument with multiple causes and specific evidence. Developing: Some argument, possibly over-focused on the Crash. Emerging: Descriptive account. SPaG: 5 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the name of the 1930 US law that imposed very high tariffs on imported goods?
Approximately how many Germans were unemployed by 1932 due to the Depression?
The Nazi Party received only 2.6 per cent of the vote in 1928 but rose to _____ per cent in July 1932.
Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 after staging the _____ incident as a pretext.
Match each event to its date.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Wall Street Crash begin?
How did the Depression break the Dawes Plan?
flashcard_questions.a: US banks recalled loans to Germany, ending the circular flow of US loans → German reparations → Allied war debt repayments

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act (1930)?
flashcard_questions.a: A US law imposing very high import tariffs, triggering retaliatory tariff increases and contracting world trade
A policy of national economic self-sufficiency, reducing dependence on international trade

flashcard_questions.q: What was Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution used for?
flashcard_questions.a: To govern Germany by presidential emergency decree, bypassing the Reichstag

flashcard_questions.q: What happened in Manchuria in September 1931?
flashcard_questions.a: Japanese Kwantung Army officers staged the Mukden incident and invaded Manchuria

flashcard_questions.q: What did the League's Lytton Commission recommend about Manchuria?
flashcard_questions.a: That Japan evacuate Manchuria and accept League supervision — which Japan rejected before withdrawing from the League

flashcard_questions.q: When was Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany?
Why did Britain leave the gold standard in 1931?
flashcard_questions.a: To devalue the pound and make British exports cheaper during the Depression

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Nazi Party's vote share in the 1928 Reichstag elections?
flashcard_questions.a: 2.6 per cent — before the Depression transformed German politics

glossary_terms.definition: A 1930 US law that imposed very high tariffs on imported goods, triggering retaliatory tariff increases by other countries and accelerating the collapse of international trade.
An economic policy adopted by several European governments in the 1930s, emphasising self-sufficiency, state control, and reduced dependence on international trade.
The constitutional device used repeatedly by German Presidents between 1930 and 1933 to govern by emergency decree, bypassing the Reichstag and weakening parliamentary democracy.
